newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-CANBERRA WATCH-Costello plays down Q4, looks to recent data.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-CANBERRA WATCH-Costello plays down Q4, looks to recent data.

text.p: Australian Treasurer Peter Costello is developing an important new message on current economic data.
The developing line is: December quarter GDP might be a little weak, but more current data shows things are fine, especially since the 1996 monetary easings haven't yet had their full effect.

That message was between the lines of two statements he made today. He said it to the regular sitting-week meeting of coalition MPs, according to the usual vague debriefing given to reporters, and then more clearly in Question Time.

The Question Time remarks were a response to today's economic releases: December quarter balance of payments (which toned down the GDP outlook) and the more boisterous numbers on retail trade and building approvals.
Here is what Costello said in parliament:
"As today's balance of payments figures note you would expect a detraction of around one percentage point from (GDP-E) growth for the December quarter national accounts.
"As a result, that will be taken in in relation to the (GDP) figures which are to be released tomorrow.
"Mr Speaker, I would however emphasise that the national accounts looking as they do to the December quarter give us a snapshot of what was happening in the economy several months ago.
"The leading indicators, including those released today of retail sales and building approvals, give you a snapshot as to what is happening in the economy now.
"Mr Speaker, it's still early days in relation to the cuts in official interest rates as they begin to come on stream.
"As you see that pickup in retail sales and confidence we would expect a picture of continuing and growing strength in the economy throughout 1997."
Note that in the third paragraph Costello introduces what he wants to "emphasise". So this is the message he is trying to get across.

Clearly he is trying to ensure that if Q4 GDP growth looks quite weak -- and the median expectation is now a very soft 0.4 percent -- then the media does not take seriously any doom-and-glooming from the Labor opposition.
But another implication is that regardless of any long bows that might be drawn from the GDP data on Wednesday, the government does not see the economy as weak.
Speculation about interest rate cuts might bear that in mind.
